Palworld developer John “Bucky” Buckley has called Crimson Desert one of the most technologically ambitious games of the past decade and urged players not to discount Pearl Abyss’s experiments over a few shortcomings.

A Pocketpair representative believes that Crimson Desert is being unfairly criticized for not conforming to conventional expectations of linear role-playing games.

Buckley shared his thoughts on the social network X while commenting on discussions surrounding the Charting the Unknown expansion. In his view, the scale of the gameplay mechanics and the technical ambition of the project deserve recognition, even if certain elements still need polishing. The developer also argued that creators should be given more room to experiment rather than constantly churning out nearly identical AAA titles.

The Pocketpair representative pointed out a contradiction in the gaming industry: companies constantly preach the need for creative freedom, yet predominantly reward safe, formulaic decisions. Crimson Desert is attempting to take a different path. Buckley prefers such risks over yet another project relying on formulas that players have been familiar with for a decade and a half.

Meanwhile, the Charting the Unknown expansion has not met with universal acclaim: around 72% of Steam reviews are positive. Players note rough edges and the need for further patches. Buckley does not consider Crimson Desert flawless, but he argues that the developers’ bold ambition deserves far more respect.

items.title: Crimson Desert is among the "most technically ambitious games we’ve seen" in 10 years but is overshadowed by "the same safe, conventional AAA games," says Palworld lead
items.content:
Open World Games Crimson Desert Crimson Desert is among the "most technically ambitious games we’ve seen" in 10 years but is overshadowed by "the same safe, conventional AAA games," says Palworld lead News By Anthony McGlynn Published 4 November 2026 "Steam reviews aren't the most glowing"

(Image credit: Pearl Abyss) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 3 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The first Crimson Desert DLC, Charting the Unknown , is here, and it's causing a stir. As reviews are published, a lead developer on Palworld is defending the fantasy sandbox, arguing that people continually underrate the game.

"Crimson Desert is one of the most technically ambitious games we’ve seen in the last decade, but because it isn’t another linear narrative RPG with the illusion of freedom, it just keeps getting underrated," John 'Bucky' Buckley, head of publishing and communications at Pocketpair, writes on Twitter .

"The technical wizardry that goes into making a game this mechanically massive is insane," he continues. "You don’t have to like every part of it, but surely the sheer ambition deserves some recognition?"

He calls this reflex "frustrating" and believes it's emblematic of a cultural trend in which people appear to want more creativity, but then "we turn around and reward the same safe, conventional AAA games over and over and over and over," in his mind.

"Crimson Desert isn’t perfect, but I’d much rather see developers attempt something genuinely ambitious and occasionally fall short than just keep making the same games we’ve been playing for the last 15 years," he adds.

Crimson Desert DLC debuts to positive Steam reviews, but it hasn't done much for PC player count Crimson Desert reviews were lower than user score due to "reviewing period" limitation, suggests CEO Crimson Desert DLC features everything from shipbuilding to marriage He got into the subject by quote-tweeting a slightly middling review of the DLC, but in the comments he mentions he finds this to be a wider issue. "There’s endless tweets moaning about Crimson Desert all over the timeline this week," he says.

Steam reviews for Charting the Unknown aren't wholly positive. Right now, the DLC has a score of 72%, with criticisms that "none of it feels finished" and it all "needs a ton more work."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Crimson Desert is a strong piece of work, but given the sales and community, I'm not sure it's really getting undersold in any forum. That said, The Game Awards are coming up, and if it's not nominated for Game of the Year, I imagine this conversation will stir back up with even more vitriol.

Crimson Desert players are sharing their best money-making grinds after the new DLC added a ship that costs more than Kliff's soul

Anthony McGlynn Social Links Navigation Contributing Writer Anthony is an Irish entertainment and games journalist, now based in Glasgow. He previously served as Senior Anime Writer at Dexerto and News Editor at The Digital Fix, on top of providing work for Variety, IGN, Den of Geek, PC Gamer, and many more. Besides Studio Ghibli, horror movies, and The Muppets, he enjoys action-RPGs, heavy metal, and pro-wrestling. He interviewed Animal once, not that he won’t stop going on about it or anything.

Recent updates August 14, 2026: I've added a new base location for farming ore and coal in the early game. It's easily one of the best spots for both, and my new favorite place to set up in a fresh save.

(Image credit: Pocketpair) (Image credit: Pocketpair) Image 1 of 2 View Original

The Sunlit Isle (405, -483) Pros: Several crude oil nodes, easy to defend during raids Cons: No nearby ore Closest teleport: Sunlit Isle It's not the best spot for ore or stone, but the Sunlit Isle just east of Palworld's starting area makes early game crude oil farming a breeze with six nodes scattered across the land. It's not difficult to defend, and the pals living here are under level 10. I like building at the highest point along the island's south side, but there's a cute spot northeast with stone steps leading up to it that works just as well. Even if you intend to go elsewhere for ore farming, this is a great place to build a second base for a steady crude oil supply.

items.title: Palworld Update Fixes The Game’s Biggest Frustration
v1.0.3: Balance Adjustments & Bug Fixes
items.summary: \ Palworld version v1.0.3 has been released! ＝＝＝ \ ▼Items and Equipment ・Changed the unlock level of some Jetragon-related technologies from 79 to 70, and reduced the materials required for the Pal Gear used to ride Jetragon. ・Changed the t
items.content:
\

Palworld version v1.0.3 has been released!

＝＝＝

\

▼Items and Equipment ・Changed the unlock level of some Jetragon-related technologies from 79 to 70, and reduced the materials required for the Pal Gear used to ride Jetragon.

・Changed the technology unlock level of the Aquatic Construction Kit from Level 66 to Level 23, changed its Ancient Technology Point requirement from 4 to 1, and adjusted the required materials and work amount.

・Extended the duration of World Tree Holy Water.

・Reduced the weight of World Tree Holy Water from 1 to 0.1.

・Added World Tree Holy Water to the rewards for World Tree expeditions, World Tree fishing, and the Large Fishing Pond.

・Increased the amount of World Tree Holy Water obtained from Pals in The World Tree area.

・Increased the amount of World Tree Holy Water obtained from Teafant Spring.

・Adjusted the work amount required to craft the Ancient Armor series.

・Doubled the amount of Fiber obtained from trees.

▼Bases and Missions

・Reduced the building costs of the Crude Oil Extractor, High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor, and Large Power Generator.

・Increased the crude oil production speed of the Crude Oil Extractor and High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor.

・The base mission that requires building a Crude Oil Extractor can now also be progressed by building a High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor.

▼Server Settings

・Added a server setting (bAllowEnemyCampSpawnNearBaseCamp) that disables the suppression of enemy camp spawns near player base camps.

\

▼Graphics and Display

・Adjusted the boundary display in some areas to make it easier to see from a distance.

・Improved the display quality of some objects in dungeons.

▼Sound

・Added a sound effect when using World Tree Holy Water.

\

▼Crashes and Progression Blockers

・Fixed an issue where the mission could become impossible to progress if the barrier was removed before accepting the main mission in Sunreach.

▼Multiplayer and Co-op

・Fixed an issue in co-op where lighting on the client side could display incorrectly after cutscenes or the ending played.

・Fixed an issue in co-op where some scenes could stutter during the cutscene that plays when entering The World Tree.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where Fast Travel could activate unintentionally during Tower Boss battles.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where Pals could appear to vibrate rapidly on the client screen.

▼Pals and NPCs

・Fixed an issue where the summoned Pal could stop fighting.

・Fixed an issue where the summoned Pal could stop helping with base work.

・Fixed an issue in multiplayer where, when the Partner Skill of Orserk or certain other Pals activated, the effect display could fail to update correctly, making it appear as though the skill had not activated.

・Fixed an issue where Alpha Surfent would not produce Leather when assigned to a Ranch.

▼Battles and Bosses

・Fixed an issue where some raid boss battles could fail to progress as intended.

・Fixed an issue where the wave effect and actual damage range did not match for some of Panthalus's attacks.

▼Bases and Building

・Fixed an issue where the placement detection for stairs and slanted roofs could fail to match their actual shape.

・Fixed an issue where stairs could not be placed correctly on the sides of foundations or roofs.

▼Items and Rewards

・Fixed an issue where the reward settings for the normal Moon Lord battle and the Ultra Raid Boss battle had not been updated to the intended settings.

・Fixed an issue where items could duplicate when performing certain actions.

・Fixed an issue where, when Katress's Partner Skill activated, switching spheres while riding could allow the player to obtain a different type of sphere.

・Fixed an issue where the World Tree Holy Water effect did not display correctly on the Pal being ridden when using World Tree Holy Water while riding.

・Fixed an issue where, after the World Tree Holy Water effect ended, riding a Pal would cause the World Tree Holy Water aura to reappear and not disappear when approaching trees in The World Tree area.

・Fixed an issue where an unintended reward was set for the desert expedition.

・Fixed an issue where the Dark Skill Fruit: Psycho Gravity did not appear on the item search screen.

・Fixed a bug where the firing interval was not set for sphere launchers

▼UI, Display, and Text

・Fixed an issue where resolution settings would not apply correctly in fullscreen mode.

・Fixed an issue where, after switching window mode with F11 / Alt+Enter, the game could unintentionally return to fullscreen mode after loading.

・Fixed an issue where, if certain effects were on screen while aiming, the entire screen could become blurred.

▼Sound

・Fixed an issue where the water sound effect could fail to play at Teafant Spring.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where the BGM for Attack Choppers triggered by other players could play even from far away.

・Adjusted the BGM playback range for Attack Choppers so that it plays correctly for players who are Wanted.

・Fixed an issue where unintended footstep sounds could play when walking on furniture or facilities.

▼Controls

・Fixed an issue where, after changing the key assignment for ""Attack that enemy!"" in Controls, selecting ""Restore to Default"" would not restore the default setting.

・Fixed an issue where settings could be applied unintentionally when interacting with the change confirmation dialog and duplicate key warning in Controls.

▼Map and Exploration

・Fixed an issue where a beach-like display could remain on the water surface after Fast Traveling to an offshore base.

＝＝＝

Thank you for your continued support of Palworld.

Palworld version v1.0.2 has been released!

This update includes improvements to gameplay stability and fixes for various issues.

＝＝＝

▼Crashes and Disconnections

・Fixed an issue where all players could be disconnected during the Panthalus battle on dedicated servers.

・Fixed an issue where players could crash during the Panthalus battle on dedicated servers.

・Fixed an issue where the Tower Boss “Victor & Shadowbeak” could disappear after using a teleportation attack during battle.

・Fixed an issue in the final boss battle where, if the host defeated the final boss while a guest was waiting to respawn, the guest’s light could fail to display correctly after respawning.

・Fixed an issue in the sub-mission “Captured Adventurer” where the screen could remain faded out if dialogue was interrupted during a fade-out sequence.

▼Achievements

・Fixed an issue where the corresponding achievement could fail to unlock even after obtaining the required Pal Effigies.

・Fixed an issue on Xbox where the icons for two Lifmunk Effigy-related achievements were using outdated versions.

▼Graphics and Display

▼Controls

・Fixed an issue where, when carrying over settings from versions earlier than v0.7, changes unrelated to Controls could still be treated as control setting conflicts.

・Fixed an issue where assigning a player action to the middle mouse button could incorrectly be treated as a conflict, preventing the setting from being applied.

・Fixed an issue where the Inventory Shortcut option was not displayed in Controls.

▼UI

▼Performance Improvements

items.title: Palworld Review – As Wide and Deep as the Ocean
items.summary: Palworld is an open world survival crafting game with creature collecting elements that is both unique and fun at a cheap price tag!
items.content:
Palworld is a 3rd person open world survival crafting game with creature-collecting elements developed and published by Pocketpair. Back in January of 2024, when the game released in early access, it was crowned as one of the biggest launches in Steam’s history , and after over a year of major updates, the game is finally officially released in its 1.0 version . But despite those years of updates, the game still looks and feels the same to me as someone who played during its early access launch.

Over the last 2 weeks of me playing it, I felt that the game is superb in what it focuses on. Whether that is the open world design and what you can do while exploring it, or the Pals that wander around that you can collect and fight with. But what it does falter in is the lack of an interesting story and just how needlessly complex the crafting and base building goes. However, despite those issues, Palworld was fun, intense, and gave me a very unique experience I was not expecting.

When you first start up Palworld, you are dropped on a beach with a few pals staring at you with a tablet nearby, talking about the “World Tree”. After this scene, you are basically thrown into the massive open world of the game. There is very little in the way of story cutscenes or any engaging story beats.

When it comes to story progression, it really is just tied to the 8 towers with bosses, and what follows after. It is all meant to get you to explore the game’s world, but there’s not really a memorable story behind it all. Just a series of going to locations, talking to people about the boss in that tower, and taking them on in a rinse-and-repeat fashion.

The bosses, however, have really cool attack patterns and arenas. Zoe, the first boss, rides atop a chaingun-wielding Pal. It’s a simple encounter, as you can use pillars in the arena to avoid gunfire. The next ones that follow, like Lily and Marcus, have more open arenas that don’t give any real space to hide but enough to maneuver around in. I think the best boss personally was Saya due to the Pal she had and the arena’s ethereal design. Saya herself, alongside the other bosses mentioned, has really cool anime-inspired designs. However, considering the lack of a real story, they couldn’t stand out besides their designs or presentation.

With all of this being said, the boss designs and how their encounters are crafted definitely make up for the lack of a real story and narrative. The epicness of the endgame bosses leans into pure cinema that will live rent-free in my mind.

A word of warning: when I said massive open world in Palworld , I meant it. This game’s world is separated into multiple giant biomes with large lakes, windy rivers, towering mountains, and cliffs that fully utilize the traversal mechanics of certain Pals. Some will let you fly, some will let you swim quickly, and some can cover ground quickly. Without them, the open world will take a very long time to get from point A to B, even with the fast travel points littered throughout.

Between all of this, you are put through the wringer on making a home, capturing Pals to do work for you, and eating to stay alive. You are taught through an NPC in the beginning area and prompts in the UI on how to get started. Chopping trees, punching and killing Pals for food, and building a Pal Box to start your first base. Palworld doesn’t really hold your hand through all of these mechanics. It lets you live and learn, even with the rarer materials and where some things come from when it comes to Pals. It’s not a problem at the beginning of the game, but when you get to the endgame tier stuff, it starts to become a little confusing.

As far as how the world is designed. Its world is designed first and foremost as beautiful, with distinct color usage. Outside of the rolling green hills and snowy valleys, there’s a volcanic area, and even sections of the game with windy caverns and crimson colored environments. It’s a visual treat, especially with some medieval flavoring as you see above with legendary Pal statues littered throughout.

Littered throughout the world are a range of different bosses, like all open worlds have. You can run into bigger, stronger versions of existing pals, or humans with threatening auras that use guns, swords, or bows and arrows. They will always offer more experience points than regular enemies, and if you capture any of the Pal mini-bosses, they are, of course, stronger than their normal counterparts.

Aside from the mini-bosses, there are random events happening in the world. You can stumble upon meteorites that have alien Pals you can capture and supply drops for enemy factions that you can steal. Not to mention oil rigs off the coasts that you can take on for extra loot as you keep exploring. As varied as the world is, you have so many random encounters to match that variety.

At the heart of the experience in Palworld is its basebuilding, and it can be either as simple as you need it to be, or as big and complex if you have the time to work your way through it all. It all starts with a single base, a Pal Box for storing your captured Pals and the space it lets you build in around it. The space is generous for each base but cannot be expanded. IF you ever feel lost on what you need to do, there’s always an upgrade path with certain things to build, leading you to the next new resource to build more facilities or armor and weapons for your character.

But the problem with the upgrade system is that, after a while, it only becomes a way of leading the player to new things. Initial upgrades add more space for Pals to be summoned, and allow for multiple bases to be placed throughout the world. But I was expecting some passive upgrades with each one past that final cap in the system. Especially when there are hundreds of different things to unlock and build, then use those things to unlock and build other things.

Despite being the deepest system in Palworld, the basebuilding becomes unnecessarily long and convoluted. I would have much preferred fewer things in the overall tech tree to unlock if they were more noticeable as upgrades. Case in point, I have a semi-auto rifle that felt similar in power to the regular laser rifle I spent more time crafting and making its ammo for. Not to mention the furnaces feel very slow when you need to build hundreds of ingots to make conveyor belts that still feel slow when building materials of Pal spheres. Speaking of Pals, though.

items.title: Palworld Review
items.summary: A clever blend of Pokemon-style creature collecting and a traditional co-op survival game.
items.content:
Before Palworld’s Early Access debut in 2024, I remember eagerly wanting to review the completely unhinged-looking “Pokemon with guns” game, mostly as a joke. Hilariously, the joke was on me when it not only became one of the biggest games of the year, but also one of my all-time favorite survival games . Two years later, with more than 160 hours spent in its 1.0 update catching colorful Pals and battling massive endgame bosses, I’m happy to report that it’s improved in almost all of the ways I hoped it would. The worst of the technical rough edges have been smoothed over, progression has been smartly streamlined, and loads of missing bits and baubles have been added. There are still plenty of parts that feel like they never got the attention they deserved during Early Access – most areas are largely empty, settlements can feel downright lifeless, and base building is still fairly janky on its best day. But on the whole, Palworld is more compelling than it’s ever been, and something I’d highly recommend for those with a taste for both creature collectors and tree-punching survival games alike.

If you’ve never played Palworld before, there’s very little I can say to prepare you for this completely bizarre adventure. You’ll recruit a roster of colorful critters who make Nintendo’s legal team furious and use them to perform unpaid labor in your work camps as you explore an increasingly dangerous world filled with gun-toting maniacs. This mix of creature collecting, open-world exploration, RPG-adjacent leveling and questing, and survival mechanics that have you building up a base to store your pals and conquer the wilds probably shouldn’t work. But it really does. And if you did play Palworld during Early Access, know that the 1.0 update fleshes out this world and the kinds of activities you tackle within it, so this over-the-top adventure now feels a lot more complete than the proof-of-concept version from two years ago.

You might assume Palworld is just a straight Pokemon ripoff at a glance, but it actually has more in common with the likes of Valheim or Grounded . After inexplicably finding yourself dropped practically naked into a world filled with magical creatures called Pals, you’ll have to build up a base and craft gear before you starve to death or freeze out in the cold, then level your way through an irresistible upgrade tree that unlocks better equipment and amenities. That climb makes it extremely easy to lose a dozen hours without noticing, as my friends and I found ourselves doing numerous times. You’ll go from swinging a club like a caveman, to crafting leather clothes and hunting with a bow, to building literal guns and ammo. Compared to your humble start, you’ll be almost unrecognizable by the endgame, sporting sci-fi armor that looks like something out of Tron and firing laser cannons at enemies from atop the back of a giant dragon.

Palworld’s twist on the familiar survival formula is how it cleverly blends in components of a creature collector, as you’ll find yourself wholly unable to survive in these harsh lands without the invaluable assistance of the critters who occupy it. By capturing Pals and putting them to work, either at your side as battle companions or at your base where they use their specific powers to perform manual labor, you quickly raise up a legion of workhorses that allow you to turn your barren campsite into an epicenter of industry. For example, a plant-based Pal named Gumoss can use its green-thumbed abilities to plant crops, while the water-based Pengullet waters them, and the sharp-clawed Cattiva harvests the produce and stores it in a nearby chest.

That automation is incredibly well-thought out and works surprisingly well, even if your dumb Pals can be a bit imprecise at times, dropping valuable materials on the floor when it’s time for bed or walking as slowly as possible to come assist you… only to turn around when they suddenly realize they’re hungry instead. So it’s not as awe-inspiringly smooth as something like Satisfactory, but what it lacks in efficiency, it makes up for in silliness and charm. The more creatures you collect, the more things you can automate at your base – but the harder you push these poor creatures, the faster their sanity will drop, until they eventually crash out and refuse to work for you. Then again, if you ever want to make an example of a slacker, you can straight up butcher your Pals for parts, squeezing the last drop of useful resources out of them in the process. Like I said, this is a super weird game, and I mean that as a compliment.

That said, while growing your base is a ton of fun, the actual act of building it has plenty of room to improve. It’s ridiculous that Palworld still lacks the ability to move items around or snap them into alignment, so you have to completely dismantle and rebuild objects if you want to move them somewhere else or just don’t like the angle they are at. The rules for structural integrity are pretty opaque as well – sometimes you’ll be told a structure lacks support despite placing down a foundation and pillars for it, and on at least one occasion I made a minor slip up by deleting the wrong piece of wall and caused my entire base to disintegrate in front of my eyes, costing me hours of progress. I seem to complain about building limitations in practically every survival game I review, so this is par for the course in a way, but it’s still aggravatingly cumbersome at times.

When you’re not putting Pals to work at your base and evolving your headquarters from a wooden shack to a high-tech factory, you’ll be venturing out into the world to capture new Pals, brave increasingly dangerous regions, and hunt for loot as you contend with psychotic human factions who often attack you on sight. Instead of just letting your party do all the fighting for you, you’re able fire pistols and stab spears into hostile Pals and human NPCs alike while your team blasts them with fireballs. It’s surprisingly fun to dodge magical blasts and then grab one of your fire-based Pals to use as a living flamethrower, especially when your friends are doing the same alongside you in co-op. It’s also a fair bit more challenging than you might think, as hostiles (especially bosses) pack a serious punch, which gives you yet another reason to excited about that new shield or piece of armor you’ve been saving all your crafting material up for.

The storyline that accompanies your climb from “naked barbarian with a stick” to “industrial sweatshop proprietor with godlike power” adds some appreciated context to what you’re doing: You’ve gotta defeat the most powerful Pal tamers in each region, then battle a vague, unspeakable evil within the center of the world tree. Sadly, this setup is mostly just used as set dressing – a stream of generic and entirely forgettable characters who direct you toward your next quest or ask you to go tick some errand off a checklist. It’s truly the bare minimum needed to string a questline together, giving you amusing tasks to complete but never actually making you feel like a part of this world. Unless you bring some friends along for the ride, you’re in for a pretty isolating adventure.

It certainly doesn’t help that Palworld has a tendency to feel fairly barren while exploring. The handful of NPC villages you’ll find are little more than small camps with a few samey merchants and quest givers hanging around, and you only really have cause to visit them either during specific quests or to buy supplies before rushing back out. The absolutely massive wild areas suffer from this same issue – although they are always filled with Pals to catch, eggs and treasure chests to hunt, and materials to collect, they otherwise feel like entirely unsettled landscapes. You’ll only rarely find NPC Pal tamers exploring the islands, aside from the generic enemy camps where poachers shoot you for no discernable reason. It’s especially weird that some vast islands exist without any clear purpose, covered with low level Pals but no real reason to explore them aside from filling out your map, which can make that process a bit of a slog at times.

But while the story and exploration can’t carry Palworld on their own, the actual action and the progression systems that drive it more than pull their weight to make up for that. This is a huge campaign that took me over 150 hours to complete (with plenty more left to do), and that marathon is paced brilliantly. It gets you into the action fast and points you toward clear objectives that push you out of your base to explore, fight bosses, and capture pals. You’re given loads of XP and access to better equipment by simply following the path in front of you, and I always felt like I was just a tiny bit ahead of the difficulty curve without needing to do much grinding. Occasionally I’d run into a high level boss that’d kick my teeth in, forcing me to regroup and work on my build, but this was a pretty rare occurrence, and one I was never annoyed by since crafting new items to overcome those hurdles was usually a fun challenge.

And although much of the map is more empty than I’d like it to be, certain areas at least have interesting barriers you’ll need to overcome before continuing your march ever outward. For example, one region is dominated by a giant volcano, so you’ll need to craft heat-resistant items to avoid catching on fire and slowly dying to the heat. Another area is suspended high in the air, accessible only by those who know a secret method to reach it. There are some cool boss fights to gate your progress, too, like one against a giant whale that throws massive tidal waves at you, requiring you to have a flying Pal at your side that can outrace the insanely tall walls of deadly water. That said, the number of memorable boss fights like this is dwarfed by the amount of forgettable ones, as most are just a matter of you and your Pals slapping around some oversized creature until it dies.

Thankfully, there is at least a good amount of choice for which Pals will do that slapping. You can battle alongside any Pals you want in order to power them up, and various consumables will upgrade them even further. It’s definitely a lot easier if you abandon your favorite Pals for ones that are naturally stronger, like the options that appear later on – legendaries and whatnot – but as someone who prefers to reject the meta and use whichever creatures I connect most with, I was impressed by how many ways Palworld provides for you to raise lesser Pals up to be viable even through to the endgame.

For example, I caught a fiery Blazamut early on in my adventure that I bonded with immediately and wouldn’t have parted with unless faced with no other option. As I leveled up, I kept finding new ways to improve my buddy’s stats, give him more powerful attacks, and buff him in various other ways – such as grinding up duplicate copies of the Pal to increase his star rating, and increasing our bond just by spending time with him in my party, both of which increased his stats. He even got strong enough that I was able to bring him into battle against post-game bosses without issue. It’s pretty awesome that this is an option, because a pet peeve of mine in other creature collectors is when everyone’s teams look identical by the end as personal flair gives way to the inescapable gravity of raw stats.

You’ll need to develop those Pals quite a bit, too, because Palworld’s endgame kicks the difficulty up to 11. It has some seriously challenging versions of each of the existing boss fights, plus raid encounters where you’ll fight alongside practically every Pal you’ve ever captured to take down a massive, deadly monster. To aid you in the effort, there’s quite a bit of equipment to unlock and rare resources to grind for even beyond the main story, and the Ancient Relic Recycler that spits out high-end resources and equipment when you claim victory against Pals in the endgame region is a particularly nice touch for speeding up the grind as you get even deeper. Some of that grind can be a bit of a pain, like hunting for randomly dropped duplicates of a schematic so you can craft a better version needed to take down a raid boss, which becomes monotonous fairly quickly. But on the whole, there’s quite a bit to chase if you’re looking to extend your time past the credits, and I happily lost way too much time doing just that.

Palworld Has Now Outsold Almost Every Mainline Pokémon Game
items.summary: Palworld has reportedly sold 30.5 million copies, surpassing almost every mainline Pokémon game, including Scarlet and Violet
items.content:
Palworld has reportedly sold 30.5 million copies, surpassing almost every mainline Pokémon game, including Scarlet and Violet

X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard Add Us On Google .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .discount{ display:none; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .discount .discount-tag{ line-height: 24px !important; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button.most-popular .join-now-button:hover { background: #000 !important; color: #fff !important; outline: 1px solid #fff !important; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .join-now-button:hover { background: 0 0; outline: 1px solid rgba(12, 12, 12, 1); color: rgba(12, 12, 12, 1); } @media (max-width: 1220px){ .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .join-now-button { width: 100% !important; position: unset !important; } } A new report claims that Palworld has sold a staggering 30.5 million units. If accurate, Pocketpair’s controversial survival game has now outsold almost every mainline Pokémon release, including Scarlet and Violet , Sword and Shield , and Gold and Silver .

According to a new report from Alinea Analytics, Palworld has now sold an estimated 30.5 million units across Xbox, PlayStation, and PC . The video game market intelligence firm also estimates that Pocketpair has generated an eye-watering $700 million in total revenue following the recent launch of Palworld 1.0.

If these latest estimates are accurate, they also mean that Palworld has now significantly outsold many of the biggest Pokémon releases over the last 30 years. In Nintendo’s most recent financial report , for example, Pokémon Scarlet and Violet only sold a combined 28.08 million units on Nintendo Switch in comparison.

However, it’s bigger than that, as Palworld has also outsold most classic Pokémon generation titles such as Gold and Silver and Gen 4’s Diamond and Pearl . Here is a full breakdown of the sales figures:

Now, there are a few factors we need to point out here. Since its launch in 1996, the mainline Pokémon series has remained exclusive to Nintendo consoles. One major advantage Palworld has is that it’s an addictive creature-catcher available across most major gaming platforms.

Alinea Analytics points out that while Palworld generated most of its revenue on PC via Steam, it also sold millions of units on PlayStation 5. The game is additionally available on Xbox and through Game Pass, giving it access to a much larger potential audience than an individual Pokémon release.

However, while Palworld has many Pokémon games beat in terms of units sold, Nintendo’s series likely generates more revenue per copy. Pokémon games typically retail for $60 to $70 at launch, while Palworld originally entered early access for $29.99 and has frequently been discounted.

Finally, Nintendo does not update Pokémon sales figures every month, meaning Scarlet and Violet has almost certainly sold additional copies since its last reported total. It’s therefore possible that the Gen 9 games are closer to Palworld than the currently available figures suggest.

Regardless, selling an estimated 30.5 million copies is an incredible achievement for a new IP that only recently debuted in 2024. Palworld is now only around 880,000 units behind Pokémon Red, Green, and Blue , which remains the best-selling mainline Pokémon generation of all time.
